An unattractive girl.
To use grenade(s) upon.
ex: They advanced after grenading the next traverse, much like the British did.

senses.d: Of an engine: to be violently wrecked so that the internal components burst out.

ety.text: Substantive use of Old French grenate in pomme grenate (“pomegranate”), from dialectal northern Italian pom granat, from Medieval Latin pomum granatum (“seeded fruit”), from Latin grānātum. The -d- developed under influence from Spanish granada.
From Latin (malum) grānātum. Compare French grenade.
From the feminine of granado, from Latin (mālum) granātum (literally “apple with many seeds”); compare granado. Compare Italian melagranata.
Italian pom granatbor. Old French pomme grenateclip. Old French grenate French grenadebor. Portuguese granada Borrowed from French grenade.
From grenade.

senses.d: Hello.
ex: Greetings and salutations. You a Heather?

ety.text: From Middle English gretnesse, gretnes, greetnesse, from Old English grēatnes. Equivalent to great + -ness.

senses.d: The state, condition, or quality of being great
ex: Due to the greatness of his size, he was an effective bodyguard.
greatness of mind

senses.d: Pride; haughtiness.
ex: It is not of pride or greatness that he cometh not aboard your ships.

grp.label: the state, condition, or quality of being great; as, greatness of size, greatness of mind, power, etc

ety.text: Inherited from Old French grandur. By surface analysis, grand + -eur.
From grande + -ezza. Compare Sicilian grannizza.
From grande + -eza.

pt:grandeza.gl: greatness (the quality of being great, big)
